title: Redis: streams & pub/sub
seriesDescription: How to use Redis in system design interviews: the data model, durability limits, clustering, caching, distributed locks, leaderboards, rate limiting, geo search, streams and pub/sub, with the trade-offs interviewers probe.
description: Work queues with streams and consumer groups, at-least-once processing, Pub/Sub delivery guarantees, sharded Pub/Sub and when to choose Kafka.
source: Study notes: how to use Redis in system design interviews

options.text: An append-only log that consumers can read from and replay.
options.why: Right: similar to a Kafka topic.

options.text: A fire-and-forget broadcast that drops messages when nobody listens.
A sorted set keyed by timestamp that cannot be read back.
A cache entry that expires after one read.
options.why: Stream entries are not consumed by reading.

questions.explanation: Producers append with XADD; consumers read and track their position.

questions.prompt: What do consumer groups add to a stream?

options.text: They coordinate which worker processes which entry and track entries pending acknowledgement.
options.why: Right: the basis for a work queue.

options.text: They copy every entry to every worker in a typical production setup.
options.why: Each entry goes to one worker in the group.

options.text: They make the stream durable regardless of persistence.
options.why: Durability still follows your persistence settings.

options.text: They remove the need for acknowledgements for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Workers acknowledge to say they are done.

questions.explanation: XREADGROUP reads, processing happens, then the worker acknowledges.

questions.prompt: A worker dies mid-task. How is the entry recovered?

options.text: Another worker claims it with XCLAIM or XAUTOCLAIM after its idle time grows.
options.why: Right: pending entries carry an idle time.

options.text: Redis re-queues it automatically the instant the worker disconnects.
The entry is deleted so the job is never run.
The producer must send it again.
options.why: The entry is already in the stream.

questions.explanation: Redis cannot tell a slow worker from a dead one, so an item can occasionally be processed twice. Make processing idempotent.

questions.prompt: When is Kafka the better choice than Redis streams?

options.text: Long retention, replay for many independent consumers, or durable ordered throughput where loss is unacceptable.
options.why: Right: that is where its complexity pays off.

options.text: When the queue is small and Redis is already in the design for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
When you need the fastest possible single-key lookups as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: That is not a messaging question.

options.text: When messages can be dropped when nobody listens.

questions.explanation: Redis streams fit background jobs, notification fan-out and work distribution at modest scale.

options.text: At-most-once delivery to subscribers connected right now.
At-least-once delivery, replayed to anyone who was offline.
Exactly-once delivery with ordering across channels.
Durable storage of every message for later replay.
options.why: That is what streams are for.

questions.explanation: It is great for ephemeral real-time notifications like chat presence or live updates.

questions.prompt: What problem does sharded Pub/Sub (SPUBLISH, SSUBSCRIBE) fix in a cluster?

options.text: Classic Pub/Sub broadcast every message to every node; sharded routes a channel to the shard that owns its slot.
options.why: Right: capacity now scales with the cluster.

options.text: It makes messages durable across restarts under normal operating conditions as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
It gives exactly-once delivery.
options.why: Delivery is still at most once.

options.text: It removes the need for subscriber connections without any extra configuration in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.

questions.explanation: Since Redis 7, adding nodes adds Pub/Sub capacity.

questions.prompt: True or false: a subscriber needs one connection per channel, so millions of channels mean millions of connections.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Connection overhead is per node: one connection carries all subscribed channels from that node.

questions.prompt: Why is building your own pub/sub on Redis keys (topic to subscriber addresses) usually worse than native Pub/Sub?

options.text: It adds a network hop, new connections per publish and heartbeat logic to clean up dead subscribers.
Native Pub/Sub stores every message forever for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
Homemade versions cannot read Redis keys.
options.why: They can; they are just slower.

options.text: Native Pub/Sub uses one connection per channel, which scales better without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: It does not use one per channel.

questions.explanation: If a use case looks like Pub/Sub, use Pub/Sub.

questions.prompt: Subscribers must catch up on messages they missed while offline. What should you use?

options.text: Redis Streams, or pair Pub/Sub with a queue or an outbox so consumers can catch up.
Plain Pub/Sub, since it replays missed messages as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
A longer TTL on the channel without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
More Pub/Sub shards.

questions.explanation: Streams give replay; SNS to SQS or Kafka give stronger guarantees.
